# v1.8.0 — The app updates itself, your setup follows you, and git gets a real home

Control Code now keeps itself up to date from GitHub Releases, in the same format you installed it. A private repository in your own git account keeps your skills and settings identical on every machine. Pull requests and issues move to a screen of their own, and the history becomes a proper branch graph with side-by-side diffs. You can also cut tags and releases without leaving the app.

> **Updating from 1.7.x:** earlier versions have no updater, so install 1.8.0 by hand once. From here on, the app offers every new version by itself.

---

## ⬆️ Updates that install themselves

About 20 seconds after launch, and every 6 hours after that, the app checks the latest release. When there is a newer one, a card appears in the bottom-right corner. It doesn't interrupt anything. The card shows:

- the version you have and the new one;
- **the release notes**, rendered, one click away;
- **Update**: downloads it with a real progress bar, **verifies its signature** and installs it in the same format you installed from:

| Installed as | Updated with |
|---|---|
| AppImage | the new AppImage |
| Windows (NSIS / MSI) | the new installer |
| macOS `.app` | the new `.app` |
| `.deb` / `.rpm` | the new package, with `pkexec` (the system asks for your password once) |

- **Restart now**: saves everything exactly like closing the app does, with the same progress dialog, and comes back on the new version.
- **Skip this version**: that version is never offered again. **GitHub** opens the release page.

*Settings → Updates* shows your version and has **Check now**.

Nothing unverifiable is ever installed. Every installer is signed in CI and checked against a public key built into the app. A build without that key still tells you about new versions. It offers the exact installer for your OS, architecture and package format, but never installs on its own.

<details>
<summary><b>What changed in the release pipeline</b></summary>

- `scripts/build.mjs` signs the installers when `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` is present. Without it, the build is exactly what it was.
- The workflow uploads the `.sig` files and renames the macOS `.app.tar.gz` per architecture, because both were produced with the same name.
- `scripts/updater-manifest.mjs` builds `latest.json` from the signed installers. It uses the keys the updater looks for (`linux-x86_64-rpm`, `windows-x86_64-nsis`, `darwin-aarch64-app`…), plus a format-less fallback per OS and architecture. Unsigned files are never listed.

</details>

## 🔄 Your skills and settings, on every machine

*Settings → Sync*: pick one of your git accounts and a repository name. If the repository already exists (another machine created it), it is used. Otherwise it is created **private**. From then on it syncs on launch, every 5 minutes and when you come back to the window, or whenever you press **Sync now**.

| Syncs | Never syncs |
|---|---|
| Skills you created or edited, whole | Tokens, TUI logins, browser cookies |
| Your skill repositories and which skills you installed from each (downloaded again on the other side) | Your custom TUIs' environment variables (they can hold keys) |
| Pre-launch commands and custom TUIs | Paths and settings of this machine (skills folder, GPU, local repositories) |
| Language, theme, terminal zoom, graphify steps, fleet tiers | Windows, tabs, sessions and the fleet |

It is a real three-way merge, not "last machine wins":

- Settings merge **key by key**, so changing the theme here and the language there keeps both.
- When the same thing changes on two machines at once, this machine wins and you're told.
- On a machine's **first** sync, the repository wins, so a fresh install doesn't overwrite your setup with defaults.
- An edit beats a deletion.
- A skill that fails to download is kept in the repository and retried, not dropped.

## 🧭 Pull requests and issues get their own screen

A new item in the rail:

- **On the left:** the repositories of your open workspaces. Several worktrees of the same repo count as one, shown with their host, account and branches. The screen starts on the repository of the active tab.
- **On the right:** **Pull requests**, **Issues** and **Releases**, each with its state filters and a "New" button.
- **Opening an item** shows it whole: description, comments, commenting, checking it out as a branch, merging.

Source Control goes back to being about your working copy: changes, commit, branches, fetch/pull/push, and now tags.

---

## 🌳 History as a graph, and diffs side by side

**The graph works like VS Code's:**

- One lane and one color per branch. Merges open and close lanes, and the main line stays on the left.
- Chips per ref: the current branch, local branches, remote branches (violet, with a cloud) and tags.
- With an upstream, you see what a pull would bring (hollow dot, ↓) and what is still to push (↑).
- Click a commit to see its files, and click a file to see that commit's diff against its parent.

**Side-by-side diffs:** the old version on the left and the new one on the right, aligned, with each side labeled. Earlier builds fell back to a unified diff because the side-by-side view froze on WebKitGTK. The folded-lines separator declared 27 px and measured 31, and the two panes kept correcting each other forever. That is fixed.

**Changes in the editor margin:**

- A green bar marks added lines, a blue bar modified ones, and a red triangle deleted ones, against the index.
- The same marks appear on the scrollbar at each change's relative position. A change halfway down the file is halfway down the bar.
- Click a mark to see what was there before, and **Revert this change** to undo just that hunk.

---

## 🏷️ Tags and releases, from the app

- **Tags:** create one (lightweight or annotated) from Source Control or right from a commit in the graph. The field proposes the next version (`v1.7.3` → `v1.7.4`). Push and delete them locally and on the remote. If the tag was created but the push failed, **Retry push** doesn't create it twice.
- **Releases:** list them, and create one from an existing or new tag, with notes, as a pre-release, or as a draft (GitHub and Gitea). Works on GitHub, GitLab and Gitea.

---

## 🤖 MCP

**Protocol**

- `ping` is answered. Strict clients used to consider the server dead.
- Every `tools/call` runs on its own thread, so the server keeps reading while a call is in progress. This enables two things:
  - **Cancellation:** `notifications/cancelled` stops the call, and `run_await` stops waiting within 2 s.
  - **Progress:** `notifications/progress` is sent every 5 s when the client passes a `progressToken`. It reports real elapsed time, not an invented percentage.
- When stdin closes, calls in flight get 5 s to finish.
- Every tool is annotated with `readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint` and `openWorldHint`.

**Permissions:** Claude Code and OpenCode now follow one rule. OpenCode used to approve every tool its config didn't mention, so launching agents or writing to the git host ran without asking. Those tools now ask first, by their full name, without overriding your own `permission` settings.

**New tools**

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `git_checks` | CI of a commit or of a PR's head (GitHub check runs and statuses, GitLab's latest pipeline, Gitea statuses) |
| `git_pr_files` | A PR's files with +/− counts, and their diff |
| `git_tag` | Create, push or delete a tag |
| `git_release_list` / `git_release_create` | Read and cut releases |
